children.note: Sorghum and the millets are small-grained cereals that feed people where maize struggles: hot, dry or poor land. They are old African crops with deep roots in Kenyan farming and cooking.
A tall grass grown for grain, malt, fodder and stems. It was first tamed in eastern Sudan more than 5,000 years ago and is now the world's fifth cereal. Swahili: mtama.

manas.q: Where was sorghum first domesticated?

children.note: Named for its head of 5–7 'fingers'. It began in the Ethiopian and Ugandan highlands and is grown in western Kenya, Uganda and India. Swahili: wimbi; also called ragi.

manas.q: Why is finger millet called 'finger' millet?

children.note: Pearl millet (very dry, sandy land), foxtail and proso millet (short season; proso needs only 200–450 mm of rain). All are small-seeded grasses.
Grain for ugali, porridge, flatbread and beer; malt for brewing; green plants and stover for livestock; stems for fencing, brooms and fuel. Thinnings also feed animals.
Both grains are gluten-free and slow to digest. Finger millet is valued for calcium and is a popular weaning porridge. Sorghum has fibre, B vitamins and minerals.

manas.q: Which mineral is finger millet especially valued for?

children.note: Sorghum is the cereal for hot, dry, uncertain seasons; finger millet suits cooler, moderately wet uplands. Choosing the right crop for the place is the first organic decision.
It can crop from about 250 mm of rain, does best above about 900 mm, and survives dry spells by rolling its leaves. It also stands short waterlogging, which maize does not.

manas.q: How does sorghum survive a dry spell?

children.note: Night temperatures below roughly 12–15 °C while sorghum flowers can leave heads empty (sterile). Frost kills it. In cold highlands use the long-season highland varieties.

manas.q: What happens if nights are very cold when sorghum flowers?

children.note: Grows on heavy black clays (vertisols) and light sands, pH about 5–8.5, and tolerates more salt than maize. It still gives grain on poor soils where other crops fail.
Best at about 18–27 °C, 500–2,400 m and well-spread rain of 500–1,000 mm, with dry weather at harvest. It copes with cooler weather than pearl millet or sorghum.

manas.q: Which tolerates cooler weather: finger millet or sorghum?

children.note: Prefers free-draining red soils that hold moisture; pH about 5–8.2. It is unusually good at using rock phosphate, a plus for organic farms.
Pick the variety by zone, season length and bird pressure. The figures are from Infonet's Kenya table; KALRO and your county office have the current seed list.
Machakos, Kitui, Makueni, Tharaka Nithi, Kajiado: Gadam, Serena, Seredo, KARI/Mtama 1 and 2, about 3–3.5 months. Gadam is a malting type that does well at low to mid altitude.
Western Kenya (Busia, Siaya, Kakamega, Kisumu, Migori) and the coffee zones: Serena, Seredo, KARI/Mtama 1. Coast: the same plus Gadam.
Nakuru, Baringo, Laikipia, Narok: long-season brown types such as E 1291, E 6518 and BJ 28 (7–8 months), dual purpose for grain and fodder.
White, sweet grains (e.g. KARI/Mtama 1) attract birds; KARI/Mtama 2 is listed as bird-resistant. Brown types suffer less but may suit fewer markets.

manas.q: Why do white sorghum varieties suffer more bird damage?

children.note: KAT/FM 1 for semi-arid lowlands, Lanet/FM 1 for cold semi-arid highlands, Gulu E for the coast and moist mid-altitudes (Infonet's Kenya list).
Small seeds need a fine, firm seedbed and timely sowing. Most losses in the first month come from poor stands, shoot fly and weeds.
Break clods after ploughing or digging; harrow once more if oxen or tractor opened the land. Prepare early so you can sow with the first rains.
Sow just before or at the onset of rains: about 5 cm deep in dry soil, 2.5–4 cm in moist soil. Early, uniform sowing also helps the crop escape shoot fly.

manas.q: How deep should sorghum be sown in dry soil?

children.note: Common: 75 cm rows, about 20 cm between plants; in Machakos–Kitui with 90 cm ox-plough rows, 15 cm in the row. Seed rate about 7–10 kg/ha (3–4 kg/acre).

manas.q: What is a common sorghum seed rate per acre?

children.note: Thin to the right stand when hand weeding. Within 2 weeks of emergence and in moist soil, transplant thinnings into gaps; extra thinnings feed livestock.
Rows of about 30 cm with 10 cm in the row, about 3 kg seed/ha. Broadcasting makes weeding nearly impossible because goosegrass looks just like young millet.

manas.q: Why sow finger millet in rows rather than broadcast?

children.note: Stir seed in 10% salt water: light, damaged and diseased seed floats and is thrown away; rinse and dry the heavy seed that sinks. A free, organic way to clean seed.

manas.q: How does a salt-water test pick good millet seed?

children.note: These crops need less than maize, but still respond to manure and legumes. Feed the soil, then let roots and microbes do the rest.
About 20 kg nitrogen and 20 kg phosphorus per hectare at planting is the guide figure; on an organic farm this comes from manure, compost and legumes.
A full farm wheelbarrow holds about 25 kg. Two per 10 × 10 m plot = 5 t/ha (low rate); four per plot = 10 t/ha (high rate). Put it in the furrows and mix with soil.

manas.q: How many wheelbarrows of manure per 10 × 10 m give about 5 t/ha?

children.note: Infonet suggests 8–10 t/ha of farmyard manure and phosphorus as rock phosphate, which finger millet uses better than most cereals.
Rotate or intercrop with beans, cowpea, pigeon pea or green gram. A global meta-analysis (462 trials) found main-crop yields about 20% higher after legumes.

manas.q: Roughly how much did legume rotations raise yields in the 2022 global meta-analysis?

children.note: Seed treatment with Azospirillum and PSB suits cereals; mycorrhiza helps phosphorus uptake on poor soils. Follow the product label.
How grass-loving nitrogen helpers work.
Making good compost for cereals.
Green manures that come before the cereal.
Weeding early decides the yield. Striga is the special enemy of sorghum and millet, and ratooning is an old trick that saves work and seed.
Weed twice: about 2–3 weeks after emergence and again two weeks later. Small-seeded millet competes poorly at first, so early weeding matters most.
Sorghum roots release sorgoleone, a natural compound that holds back some weeds, especially in narrow rows. It helps, but does not replace weeding.

manas.q: What weed-suppressing compound do sorghum roots release?

children.note: A parasitic plant that taps sorghum roots and steals water and food; bad fields can be abandoned. Most damage is done underground before the pink flowers appear.

manas.q: Why is Striga damage often done before you see the weed?

children.note: Pull Striga before it sets seed, build soil fertility, intercrop with legumes, and use push–pull with desmodium, which suppresses Striga almost completely. Resistant lines exist (ICRISAT).
Desmodium, Brachiaria and the full layout.
Cut the harvested stalks and let them regrow for a second crop. In Eastern Kenya, short-rains sorghum cut in February regrows for the March rains; thin to 2–3 tillers per hill.

manas.q: Why does a ratoon sorghum crop start faster than a newly sown crop?

children.note: The roots are already in place to use soil water early; it saves ploughing, seed and labour, and the early crop can mature before quelea flocks arrive.
Most damage comes from shoot fly at the start, stemborers in the middle, and birds and head caterpillars at the end. Organic control is timing, resistant varieties and natural enemies.
A small grey fly whose maggot kills the growing point: the 'dead heart' leaf pulls out easily and smells bad. Seedlings in the first month are at risk.

manas.q: What is a 'dead heart' in sorghum?

children.note: Sow early and all at once with neighbours, use a slightly higher seed rate, grow varieties that recover (Serena, Seredo), destroy old stubble, and protect spiders and parasitic wasps.
Spotted stemborer and African stalkborer. Early sign: rows of small holes across the newest leaves — act then, before larvae enter the stem.

manas.q: What is the early warning sign of stemborers?

children.note: Mix ground neem seed 1:1 with dry clay or sawdust and drop a pinch into the leaf funnel; about 1 kg treats 1,500–2,000 plants. Push–pull and residue destruction help too.
African bollworm eats grain in compact heads from the milk stage. Shake heads over a bucket weekly after flowering; hand-pick or spray Bt or neem early.
In outbreak years caterpillars strip young plants. Check field edges daily in risky weather; Bt, neem or pyrethrum work only while caterpillars are small.
Red-billed quelea flocks can strip a field. Scare birds away during grain fill, grow brown or bird-resistant types, and time harvests to avoid flock season.

manas.q: Name two organic ways to reduce quelea damage.

children.note: Stemborers, armyworms and bollworms in depth.
Most sorghum and millet diseases are prevented with clean seed, resistant varieties, rotation away from cereals, and burying or removing old residues.
Covered and loose kernel smut replace grains with sacs of black spores; both are seed-borne. Use clean, certified seed and rotate with non-cereals.

manas.q: How do kernel smuts reach the next crop?

children.note: Sticky cream-to-pink 'honeydew' drips from flowers, then dark sclerotia replace grains. Favoured by humid (RH > 80%), 20–30 °C weather at flowering. Remove heads; never save their seed.

manas.q: What does ergot look like on a sorghum head?

children.note: Small round leaf spots with straw centres and red-purple margins; inside the stalk below the head the pith turns brick-red, and grain fills poorly. Use resistant varieties and rotate.
Post-flowering heat and drought let this soil fungus shred the pith; plants lodge and the split stalk looks dusted with pepper. Avoid moisture stress; mulch and manage residues.

manas.q: What weather favours charcoal rot?

children.note: Grey-centred diamond spots, neck and finger rot; losses up to 80% reported in bad years in Uganda. Rotate, bury infected straw, wash tools, weed grass hosts, avoid dense stands.

manas.q: Name three cultural controls for finger millet blast.

children.note: Chemical seed dressings and systemic fungicides used on conventional farms are not permitted under organic standards. Check any product with your certifier.
Harvest at the right moment, dry well, and these grains keep a long time. Finger millet can be stored for years — a famine reserve.
At physiological maturity the grain is hard and gives no milk when pressed. Cut heads with a knife or sickle.

manas.q: How can you tell sorghum grain is mature?

children.note: Sun-dry heads before threshing and store grain at about 12–13% moisture; dry grain resists weevils, beetles and moths.
Millet ripens unevenly: cut when the main ear and half the ears are brown, then the rest a week later; dry the green heads in shade. Late harvest loses seed.

manas.q: Why is millet often harvested in two passes?

children.note: Rice weevil, flour beetle and the grain moth attack stored sorghum. Dry grain, hard-grained varieties and clean, sealed stores are the organic defence.
Finger millet's tiny grain is hardly attacked by insects and keeps up to about five years when dry — why it was a famine store.
Weevils, moths and hermetic storage.
Small grains are coming back as climate change hits maize. Kenya's dry counties and western Kenya are the main areas; India is the world's biggest millet grower.
They yield where maize fails in drought years, need fewer inputs, and store well — strong reasons in Kenya's arid and semi-arid lands.
Malting types such as Gadam are sold to brewers; check current contract terms and prices with buyers and your county office before planting.
Sorghum (jowar) and millets (ragi, bajra) are major dryland crops; improved varieties from ICRISAT spread widely there.
Broadcast millet cannot be told apart from goosegrass when young, so weeds win. Sow in rows.
Seed from smutted or ergot-infected heads carries disease into the next season. Save seed only from clean, healthy heads.
